I shipped our early validation workflows assuming client connections were stable, but long-running scenario suites quickly exposed that fragile assumption. When an agent triggers a deep verification pass, tying the entire execution to the client session creates an artificial failure path where a simple disconnect invalidates the test run.

To eliminate this gap, we updated test-genie, our scenario testing engine, to take complete ownership of a scenario test run the moment the initiating command returns. This shift establishes a durable, server-owned lifecycle that outlives caller disconnections.

Because test-genie manages the run independently, the execution preserves its unique identity, operational logs, and final evidence on the server. The builder no longer needs to keep a persistent terminal attached just to safeguard the suite's progress.

Instead of treating connection drops as test errors, the system ensures validation continues securely, allowing operators to trigger long suites and wait on durable evidence with confidence.

When we shipped the execution loop for long validations, our primary goal was eliminating false alarms caused by dropped connections. As a builder, nothing frustrates a release pipeline more than losing hours of execution data just because an interactive terminal closed unexpectedly.

The operational mechanics we designed are deliberate and lean. An operator starts the scenario suite through our orchestration service, test-genie, which immediately accepts the execution payload and returns control to the caller. At that exact point, the operator records the unique run identifier emitted by the command. Instead of holding open a brittle, continuous stream, the client only needs to execute a single wait call against the server-owned run whenever it is ready to check status.

This simple sequence protects the integrity of our test telemetry. Because test-genie owns the execution lifecycle from the moment the trigger returns, a cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. If an agent session drops, the scenario continues to execute on the server without interruption, maintaining its active logs and state transitions.

Separating the client transport from the execution lifecycle fundamentally changes how we diagnose issues. When an interactive session dies, traditional harnesses mark the validation as broken, muddying the water between network blips and software bugs. With a server-owned run, that confusion disappears. If a test fails, we know it reached a genuine failure path in the product, not a dropped socket. The resulting evidence remains intact and verifiable on the server, ready for inspection regardless of what happened to the local terminal.

When a validation pass spans multiple hours, waiting cannot remain an unmanaged side effect of an open shell. I shipped this architecture so that waiting becomes a governed, verifiable capability rather than a fragile hope that nothing drops.

In our setup, the background execution manager we call test-genie takes custody of the scenario suite immediately after invocation. Because execution is fully server-owned, the lifecycle of the suite decouples from whichever agent triggered it.

This separation changes how team handoffs work. An engineer can kick off a suite, log the run identifier, and step away. When a new shift begins, the incoming builder does not need to guess whether an interrupted connection was an infrastructure hiccup or a true product defect. They simply wait on the existing identifier, inspect the preserved logs, and evaluate genuine failure path evidence.

Ultimately, governance is about making decisions from durable ground truth. With persistent server-owned runs, validation continues uninterrupted, giving every operator reliable evidence whenever they check in.
baseline_text:
# Durable validation is a product capability

Vrooli's test-genie owns a scenario test run after the command returns. That matters when a suite takes longer than an agent session: the run keeps its identity, logs, and result instead of disappearing with the caller.

The workflow is simple. Start the scenario suite, record the run identifier, and wait once on the server-owned run. A cancelled client is not the same thing as an aborted run. This gives operators durable evidence for long-running validation and makes a later handoff possible.

The distinction is operational, not cosmetic. A system that treats every disconnected terminal as a failed test loses the difference between infrastructure interruption and a product defect. Server-owned runs preserve that distinction so the next operator can inspect the evidence and make a grounded decision.

The result is a control plane that can improve itself without asking every agent to stay attached to a terminal. Durable runs turn waiting into a governed capability: the work continues, the evidence remains addressable, and the final decision can be made from the same record that produced it.
